can you give some facts on why i eat more when i dont train and then need more insulin that make me hungrier
Short Answer: First, the food volume is supposed to look like a lot. That is the secret weapon to beating the exact insulin-hunger cycle you are trapped in right now. Eating a massive pile of broccoli physically stretches your stomach, which makes you feel full without requiring any extra insulin.
When you don't train, you fall into a vicious biological trap where eating leads to insulin, and insulin leads to extreme hunger. Here are the exact facts on why this happens:
Fact 1: The "Rest Day" Ghrelin Rebound
The Biology: When you play football or lift heavy, your body is in "fight or flight" mode. It temporarily shuts down your digestive system and suppresses ghrelin (the hormone that makes you hungry) so you can focus on moving.
The Result: On rest days, that suppression is gone. Plus, your body is burning energy trying to repair the muscle damage from the day before. Your brain cranks up the ghrelin, making you feel naturally hungrier when you are just sitting around.
Fact 2: The Insulin "False Alarm" Crash
The Biology: When you eat more food (especially carbohydrates) to satisfy that rest-day hunger, you have to inject more mealtime insulin.
The Result: Insulin's only job is to aggressively pull sugar out of your blood. If that large dose of insulin drops your blood sugar quickly—even if it just drops it from an 8.0 down to a normal 5.0—your brain panics. It senses the speed of the drop, assumes you are about to have a hypo, and blasts you with intense, ravenous hunger to force you to eat and catch the fall.
Fact 3: The "Fullness" Blockade (Leptin Resistance)
The Biology: Leptin is the hormone that your stomach sends to your brain to say, "Stop eating, we are full."
The Result: High levels of circulating insulin actually block leptin signals in the brain. When you take a large dose of insulin for a big rest-day meal, your brain literally cannot hear your stomach telling it that you are full. You can eat a massive plate of food and still feel like you are starving 20 minutes later.

Here is a draft for your blog post. It takes the hard biological facts of the insulin-hunger cycle and translates them into an engaging, relatable article for anyone struggling with rest-day cravings.
The Rest-Day Hunger Trap: Why More Insulin Equals More Cravings
Ever notice how on the days you push yourself to the absolute limit on the pitch or in the gym, you can easily stick to your diet—but the second you take a "rest day," you feel like you could eat the entire kitchen?
It is a frustrating paradox. You are doing less, burning less, yet your stomach is demanding more.
For those of us managing our blood sugar and insulin, this isn't just a willpower issue. It is a biological trap where eating leads to taking more insulin, and taking more insulin leads to extreme, ravenous hunger.
Here is the science behind why you are starving on your days off, and exactly how to break the cycle.
1. The Ghrelin Rebound
When you are playing a heavy match of football or lifting heavy weights, your body enters a mild "fight or flight" state. To keep you focused on moving and surviving, your brain temporarily shuts down your digestive system and suppresses ghrelin (your body's primary hunger hormone).
When you take a rest day, that suppression is completely lifted. Combine that with the fact that your body is burning energy behind the scenes to repair your damaged muscle tissue, and your brain cranks the ghrelin dial up to ten. You feel naturally hungrier precisely because you are sitting still and recovering.
2. The Insulin "False Alarm" Crash
Here is where the real trap begins. You feel hungry on your rest day, so you eat a larger, carb-heavy meal. To cover that meal, you have to inject a larger dose of mealtime insulin.
Insulin has one job: aggressively pull sugar out of your bloodstream. If that large dose of insulin drops your blood sugar quickly—even if it is just dropping it from a slightly elevated level down to a perfectly normal one—your brain panics. It senses the speed of the drop, assumes you are about to crash into a dangerous low, and blasts you with intense, ravenous hunger to force you to eat and "catch" the fall.
3. The "Fullness" Blockade (Leptin Resistance)
Have you ever eaten a massive plate of food, taken your insulin, and still felt like you were starving 20 minutes later? You aren't crazy; your brain is literally locked out.
Leptin is the hormone your stomach sends to your brain to say, "Stop eating, we are full." However, high levels of circulating insulin actually block leptin signals from entering the brain. When you take a large dose of insulin for a big rest-day meal, your brain physically cannot hear your stomach telling it that you are full.
How to Break the Cycle
You cannot out-willpower your own hormones, but you can outsmart them. The secret weapon is Volume Eating.
On your rest days, you have to remove the dense, insulin-spiking carbohydrates (like rice, pasta, or bread) and replace them with massive, oversized portions of fibrous green vegetables and lean protein.
The Stretch: Eating a massive pile of broccoli physically stretches your stomach, which triggers a fullness response without needing carbs.
The Flatline: Lean proteins and green vegetables require very little to no rapid-acting insulin.
The Result: Less insulin means no rapid blood sugar drops. No rapid blood sugar drops means your brain never triggers that panic-hunger.
You get to eat a physically huge plate of food, keep your insulin doses incredibly low, and finally escape the rest-day hunger trap.

Deadlifting is an incredible strength builder, but placing a heavy session exactly 32 hours before a football match is a massive biomechanical trap.
Here is exactly why keeping deadlifts off today's menu protects your legs and your performance:
1. The Hamstring Overload
The Lift: Deadlifts place a massive eccentric load on your hamstrings and glutes, creating micro-tears in the muscle fibers that take 48 to 72 hours to heal.
The Match: Sprinting in football requires your hamstrings to fire explosively to decelerate your legs. If those muscles are already fatigued and micro-torn from deadlifts, they cannot absorb the shock of a sudden sprint or change of direction, making a pulled or torn hamstring highly likely.
2. The Nervous System Drain
Lifting heavy weight off the floor taxes your Central Nervous System (CNS) more than any other exercise.
A fatigued CNS means your brain cannot send electrical signals to your muscles as fast as usual. Tomorrow night, your legs will literally feel like they are moving through wet concrete, and your reaction time to the ball will be a fraction of a second too slow.
National Institutes of Health (.gov)

Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness (DOMS) usually peaks on the second day. If you deadlift at 1:00 PM today, that stiffness and tightness will hit its absolute maximum right around 8:00 PM tomorrow—exactly when the referee blows the whistle.
The Tactical Swap
To keep your legs fresh and explosive for Sunday, treat today as an upper-body or very light accessory day.

Short Answer: To replicate the heavy pulling power of a deadlift without frying your legs for tomorrow's match, we need to completely isolate your upper back.
Since the deadlift is primarily a posterior chain (back and hamstrings) movement, we are going to drop the hamstrings out of the equation entirely. Here are the three best alternatives you can swap into your 5x5 right now to build raw strength while keeping your legs 100% fresh.
1. The Direct Swap: Seated Cable Rows (Heavy 5x5)
The Setup: Load up the V-bar or wide grip on the seated cable machine.
Why it Works: You are still pulling massive amounts of weight horizontally, which thickens your mid-back and lats just like a deadlift. Because you are seated, your legs and lower back are completely braced and removed from the equation. Zero hamstring strain.
2. The Barbell Alternative: Chest-Supported Dumbbell Rows
The Setup: Set an incline bench to about 45 degrees. Lie face down on it with a heavy dumbbell in each hand and row them up to your ribs.
Why it Works: Standard barbell rows still require your hamstrings and lower back to stabilize your torso. By lying face down on the incline bench, the bench supports your entire body weight. You get the heavy free-weight stimulus with absolutely zero central nervous system or lower-body fatigue.
3. The Vertical Pull: Weighted Lat Pulldowns (Heavy 5x5)
The Setup: Lock your knees firmly under the pads and pull the wide bar down to your upper chest.
Why it Works: Deadlifts build incredible lat strength. Heavy, low-rep lat pulldowns give you that exact same upper-back width and power, but because the weight is pulling you up, your legs do zero work.

1. Exercise Endocrinology & Insulin Dynamics

2. The Neurobiology of Satiety & The Rest-Day Trap
Exercise-Induced Anorexia (Ghrelin Suppression): Acute, high-intensity exercise temporarily suppresses ghrelin (the primary hunger hormone) and redirects blood flow away from the splanchnic (digestive) bed. On rest days, this suppression is lifted, causing a biological rebound in appetite.

Mechanoreceptor Activation (Volume Eating): Ingesting low-calorie, high-volume fibrous vegetables physically stretches the gastric wall. CNS Fatigue & Fast-Twitch Inhibition: Max-effort compound lifts heavily tax the central nervous system, reducing the speed and efficiency of electrical signals sent to the muscles. Attempting explosive, fast-twitch movements (sprinting) while the CNS is fatigued and the hamstrings are micro-torn drastically increases the statistical probability of a muscle avulsion or strain.

Here are the three best alternatives for Day 2 to replace the pull-up/pulldown:
1. The Power Swap: Plate-Loaded High Row Machine (5x5)
The Setup: Most commercial gyms have an Iso-Lateral High Row machine (often Hammer Strength). You sit facing the pad and pull the handles down and back from a high angle.
Why it Works: This is the absolute best 5x5 substitute. It allows you to safely load massive amounts of weight (like a pulldown) but changes the angle of the pull from purely vertical to diagonal. It heavily targets the upper lats and the lower traps, giving you that thick, wide back without requiring the bodyweight mastery of a pull-up.
2. The Bodyweight Bridge: Rack Chins (5x5)
The Setup: Set a barbell in a squat rack (or use a Smith Machine) at about chest height. Place a bench in front of it. Hang from the bar, put your heels on the bench so your body makes an "L" shape, and pull your chest to the bar.
Why it Works: This is the ultimate bridge to learning pull-ups. Because your feet are supported, you are only pulling about 50% to 60% of your body weight, allowing you to easily hit 5 reps. It mimics the exact vertical pulling mechanics of a pull-up but entirely removes the lower-body deadweight.
3. The Unilateral Option: Half-Kneeling Single-Arm Cable Pulldown (5x5 per arm)
The Setup: Attach a single D-handle to the top of a cable pulley. Drop down onto one knee (the knee on the same side as your pulling arm should be on the floor). Pull the cable down, driving your elbow into your hip.
Why it Works: By doing one arm at a time, you allow your shoulder blade to move much more freely than when both hands are locked onto a straight bar. This is incredibly healthy for your shoulder joints and allows for a much deeper, more intense contraction in the lat.

Here is the exact biology of why frequent, low-impact running makes your legs feel significantly looser and healthier:
1. Mechanotransduction (Aligning the Scar Tissue)
The Biology: When a muscle tears, the body patches it with collagen (scar tissue). If you just sit on the couch, that collagen forms in a messy, chaotic web (like a pile of dropped twigs). This chaotic web physically binds the muscle together, making it feel incredibly stiff and tight.
The Fix: When you do frequent, light jogging, the physical movement sends a mechanical signal to your cells (mechanotransduction). It forces those chaotic collagen twigs to align perfectly parallel with your healthy muscle fibers. This restores the elastic stretch to the muscle, completely removing that tight, stiff sensation.
2. The "Muscle Pump" (Metabolic Flushing)
The Biology: Heavy superset workouts and intense football matches leave a massive amount of metabolic waste (hydrogen ions, dead cellular debris) trapped in the local muscle tissue.
The Fix: The heart alone cannot clear all of this waste from your lower body. Your calf and hamstring muscles act as secondary "pumps." Frequent, light running physically squeezes the veins in your legs, flushing the stagnant waste fluid out and forcefully pumping highly oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood back into the healing tissues.
3. Synovial Fluid Circulation (The Joint Lube)
The Biology: Your knees and hips do not have a direct blood supply to their internal cartilage. They rely on "synovial fluid" for lubrication and nutrition.
The Fix: Synovial fluid behaves like a non-Newtonian fluid (like ketchup). When you are sitting still, it becomes thick, viscous, and gel-like, making your joints feel stiff and creaky. The repeated, gentle impact of a treadmill jog literally heats up and agitates the fluid, turning it into a slick, watery lubricant that makes your joints glide effortlessly.
4. Neurological Down-Regulation
The Biology: Stiffness is not just a physical problem; it is a neurological alarm system. Your brain creates a sensation of "stiffness" around an injury to prevent you from moving it and causing more damage.
The Fix: By frequently stepping on the treadmill and running safely (short strides, controlled environment), you are proving to your Central Nervous System (CNS) that the leg is structurally sound. Once the brain realizes the tissue is not under threat, it turns off the neurological "stiffness" alarm, allowing the muscles to relax.

The Complication: Because you have to manually inject exogenous insulin, your levels are often circulating higher than a non-diabetic's would be at rest. For you, the math is a constant, high-stakes balancing act between matching your enzymes to your macros, timing your insulin so it doesn't lock your fat cells shut during a workout, and avoiding the "hypo tax" that ruins the deficit.

The Target: You are aiming for 8 to 10 reps on your primary heavy lifts (like the Flat Bench or Incline Press).
The Test: Grab the 27.5kg or 30kg dumbbells. If you can easily push out 12 reps, the weight is still too light. If you physically cannot lift the dumbbells past 6 reps, it is too heavy.
The Sweet Spot: You want a weight where the 8th or 9th rep feels like a massive struggle, but you know you could do one or two more if a gun was to your head. Stop there. You leave exactly two reps in the tank. This triggers muscle preservation without destroying your recovery.
2. The Rest Protocol (The 90-Second Engine)
This is where the fat loss actually happens. How you rest dictates whether you are building a VO2 engine or just taking a nap on the bench.
Inside the Superset (0 Seconds): When you finish your 8 to 10 reps of the DB Bench Press, you do not check your phone or grab a drink. You immediately squeeze the dumbbells together and start your Close-Grip Press. Zero rest. This spikes your heart rate into that 140+ BPM zone.
After the Superset (90 Seconds): Once both exercises are done, start your watch. You get exactly 90 seconds of total rest. This is just enough time to let the lactic acid clear and your heart rate drop back down to around 110 BPM. The second the clock hits 90, you pick the weights back up for Set 2.
3. The "A vs. B" Weight Drop
You will likely need two different sets of dumbbells at your station.
Your "A" exercise (the primary lift, like the Seated Shoulder Press) will use your heavier weights.
Your "B" exercise (the immediate follow-up, like the Lateral Raises) will require significantly lighter weights. Because your muscles are already pre-exhausted from the first movement, a 10kg or 12kg dumbbell will suddenly feel like 25kg. Check your ego at the door on the "B" exercises; focus entirely on the stretch and the squeeze.
Now that you have the exact exertion targets and the 90-second rest clock locked in to keep the heart rate elevated, do you want to map out that safe, machine-based Thursday Leg Day to complete the entire 5-day lifting schedule?
alternative ti incline push up
Short Answer: If your wrists are fried or you simply hate push-ups at the end of a heavy session, we can easily swap them for a dumbbell-only chest burnout that keeps you glued to your bench without losing your spot.
Incline push-ups (hands on the bench) are typically used to hit the lower/mid chest and completely exhaust the muscle safely. We can achieve that exact same metabolic burnout with dumbbells using pure tension.
Here are the two best free-weight alternatives to replace the push-ups in your Friday Station 3 Finisher. Pick the one that feels best on your joints:
Alternative 1: The Lying Dumbbell "Hex Press" (Squeeze Press)
This is the ultimate chest burnout if you don't have access to cable machines. It relies entirely on inward tension.
The Setup: Lie flat on your bench. Instead of holding two dumbbells, grab one moderately heavy dumbbell.
The Execution: Hold the dumbbell sideways, pressing the palms of your hands flat against the weighted "hex" heads (like you are trying to crush the dumbbell between your hands).
The Burn: Keep squeezing your hands together as hard as you can, and press the dumbbell straight up over your chest. Lower it to your sternum and repeat. Because you are physically forcing your hands inward the entire time, it floods the chest with blood and creates a massive pump with zero strain on the shoulder joints.
Alternative 2: The Dumbbell Floor Press
If your chest is completely dead and you want a highly stable pressing movement that protects the shoulders.
The Setup: Grab a pair of lighter dumbbells, slide off your bench, and lie flat on the floor right next to it.
The Execution: Press the dumbbells up exactly like a standard bench press.
The Burn: Because the floor physically stops your elbows from dropping past your torso, it completely removes the stretch from the shoulder capsule. All of the pressing power has to come from the triceps and the chest pushing from a dead stop. You just rep it out to absolute failure.
Your New Friday Finisher (Station 3)
You just drop whichever alternative you choose right into the 3rd block on Friday.
3 Sets to Absolute Failure:
The Hex Press OR Dumbbell Floor Press (Chest burnout).
Dumbbell Tricep Kickbacks (Immediately stand up, bend over, and flush the triceps with light weight).
Now that the upper-body matrix is completely bulletproofed and customized to your exact equipment preferences, are we ready to build that safe, machine-based Thursday Leg Day so your lower body is completely recovered for Friday badminton and Sunday football?

So how best to deal with blood sugar when playing football, is better to have it in my muscles as glucagon or glyacgon,it's high at the moment should I take insulin the game is 2 h 45 from the start of the game. Currently about 13 mmol
Short Answer: Do not take the insulin right now. 13 mmol/L is actually the perfect defensive buffer for a high-intensity football match. If you inject a correction dose now, that insulin will still be active the second you step onto the pitch, putting you at massive risk for a mid-game crash.
First, let's quickly clear up the biology so you know exactly what is happening in your body:
Glycogen is the sugar physically stored inside your muscles for explosive energy. Yes, you want your muscles completely packed with glycogen for football.
Glucagon is the emergency hormone your pancreas is supposed to release to save you from a blood sugar crash. Because your pancreas doesn't make glucagon anymore, you have no biological parachute.
Because you lack that parachute, managing a football match requires exploiting the numbers to your advantage. Here is exactly why you ride the 13 mmol/L into the game and keep the insulin pen in your bag.
1. The "Active Tail" Trap (The 2h 45m Window)
If you take rapid-acting insulin right now, it hits its absolute peak effect in about 1.5 to 2 hours.
Right at kickoff, you will still be squarely in the "active tail" of that dose.
The second you start sprinting, your muscle cells unlock and become hyper-sensitive, instantly sucking the glucose out of your blood. If there is any active exogenous insulin floating around while you sprint, your blood sugar will plummet, and you will be forced to sit on the sideline eating jelly babies instead of playing.
2. The Safe Play Zone (The 13 mmol/L Shield)
Clinical sports guidelines state the safe starting zone for a diabetic athlete is between 5.0 and 13.9 mmol/L.
Sitting at 13 right now is not a failure; it is your ultimate shield. It gives your muscles a massive pool of circulating glucose to burn through during the heavy sprints and physical tackles of the first half, without dropping you into the danger zone.
3. The Adrenaline Factor
Football is an aggressive, anaerobic sport. When you tackle, sprint, and compete, your body dumps adrenaline.
Adrenaline actively signals your liver to dump its stored sugar into your blood. Do not be surprised if you check your monitor at halftime or full-time and you are sitting at 14 or 15 mmol/L. This is a normal, mechanical stress response, not a sign that your diet failed.
The Game Plan
Hydrate: Drink plenty of water between now and kickoff. Water helps your kidneys naturally filter out some of the excess glucose without the need for an insulin injection.

When you have Type 3c, carbs are a double-edged sword. Eat too many, and you spike your blood sugar and gain fat. Eat too few without adjusting your medication, and the lack of a glucagon parachute means you hit a severe, dangerous low.
Add the ADHD brain to the mix, and cutting carbs too aggressively can trigger the exact dopamine-starved binges we are trying to stop.
If you want to pull the carbs down to accelerate the fat loss safely, here is the exact protocol to protect your brain, your engine, and your blood sugar.
1. The Insulin Rule (The Non-Negotiable)
If you are dropping your carbohydrate intake, your rapid-acting insulin doses must drop with it.
The Danger: If you eat a low-carb meal (like chicken and broccoli) but take your "normal" dose of rapid-acting insulin out of habit, that insulin has no food to absorb. It will immediately attack your bloodstream, dropping you into a severe hypo.
The Rule: You must meticulously match your rapid-acting insulin strictly to the carbs you actually consume. If a meal has near-zero carbs, it likely requires near-zero rapid-acting insulin.
2. Targeted Carbs (Fueling the Matches)
You cannot play explosive, stop-and-go football on zero carbs. Your fast-twitch muscle fibers require glycogen to sprint.
Match Days (Sunday & Monday): Do not go low carb on these days. Stick to the Front-Loaded Protocol we discussed. Eat your heavy carbs (rice, oats, potatoes) at midday with your proper insulin dose. Let the insulin clear, and play the evening match on a full tank of glycogen but zero active insulin.

3. The Rest Day Strategy (Surviving the Void)

The Volume Hack: If you remove carbs (which are physically bulky and comforting) on a rest day, you must replace them with massive, stomach-stretching volume.
The Execution: Think gigantic bowls of leafy greens, roasted cauliflower, courgettes, and massive portions of lean meat. You have to physically stretch the stomach lining to send a "fullness" signal to the brain, otherwise the chemical craving for a high-carb binge will completely override your willpower.
4. The Hydration Trap
Carbohydrates physically hold water in your muscles (1 gram of carb holds about 3 grams of water).
When you go low carb, your body flushes all of that water and the essential sodium out through your kidneys. This is the "water weight" people lose in week one.
The Fix: If you go low carb, you must aggressively increase your salt and water intake, especially before your gym sessions. If you don't, your blood volume drops, you will feel dizzy, your heart will race, and your performance will completely stall.
By placing your carbs strategically around your most intense athletic events and keeping them low the rest of the week, you force your body to burn fat without triggering a starvation response.

Is that true about calories where do they go
Short Answer: Yes, it is 100% true. It sounds like fake fitness math, but it is pure biological thermodynamics. Those calories physically leave your body as heat.
When you hear that your body "burns" calories digesting protein, it can be hard to visualize where those calories actually disappear to. They don't just vanish into thin air; they are spent as physical energy to do mechanical and chemical work inside your gut.
Here is exactly where those calories go and why protein is the most "expensive" food for your body to process.
The Biological Overhead (Thermic Effect of Food)
Every time you eat, your body has to spend energy to break the food down into usable parts. This is called the Thermic Effect of Food (TEF). Different macros cost different amounts to process:
Dietary Fat (0% to 3% Cost): Fat is incredibly easy for your body to process. If you eat 100 calories of butter, your body keeps about 98 of them.
Carbohydrates (5% to 10% Cost): Carbs are slightly more complex, but still an easy, preferred fuel source.
Protein (20% to 30% Cost): Protein molecules are massive, complex chains held together by strong nitrogen bonds. Your body hates breaking these apart because it is incredibly hard work.
Where the Calories Physically Go
When you eat 200 grams of protein, your body has to go into biochemical overdrive to dismantle it into individual amino acids. Here is where the "missing" 200+ calories are physically spent:
Organ Fuel: Your stomach and intestines have to physically churn and contract much harder and longer to grind down heavy meats and dense proteins. That muscular action requires cellular energy (ATP).
Enzyme Production: Your pancreas and stomach have to manufacture and pump out massive amounts of digestive enzymes and stomach acid to dissolve the nitrogen bonds. Creating those chemicals costs calories.
Released as Heat: The chemical reactions required to dismantle protein are highly inefficient and produce a massive amount of internal heat. (This is why some people get the "meat sweats" after eating a massive steak). Those calories are physically radiated off your skin into the air as heat.
The Net Result on Your 1,700 Calorie Day
Because you hit 200 grams of protein (which is 800 total calories of protein), your body was forced to spend roughly 200 of those calories just running the digestive machinery.
Those 200 calories were burned off as body heat and internal organ work, leaving you with a "net" energy intake that is actually much lower than the 1,700 you logged on paper. You essentially forced your body to do a light cardio session entirely through digestion.

Here is how to use Skullcrushers to get that exact same muscle-building stretch without touching your headphones, plus one cable alternative for your longer Wednesday/Thursday sessions.
1. The "Modified" Dumbbell Skullcrusher
Standard Skullcrushers have you lowering the weight directly to your forehead. To make it even more effective for the long head of the triceps (and completely clear of your headphones), make this one mechanical tweak:

2. The Cable Cross-Body Extension (For Your Long Day)

Should I split my basal?
Short Answer: Splitting a basal dose (taking half in the morning and half at night) is a highly effective strategy to create a perfectly flat baseline, but at your newly lowered 15-unit dose, you have to watch out for a specific biological catch regarding how long the insulin actually lasts.
Whether or not you should split your dose depends entirely on what your LibreLink graph is doing in the 4 to 6 hours right before your next scheduled injection.
Here is the exact mechanical breakdown of why people split their background insulin, the risks of splitting smaller doses, and how to know if your engine needs it.
1. The "24-Hour" Myth and the Coverage Gap
Many long-acting insulins claim to last a full 24 hours. In biological reality, they often run out of gas around the 18 to 20-hour mark.
If you take your 15 units at 10:00 PM, the insulin is actively catching the liver's sugar drip all night and through the next day.
However, by 6:00 PM the next evening, that insulin might be completely worn off.
Because your liver never stops dripping sugar, your blood sugar will start inexplicably climbing in the hours right before bed, even if you haven't eaten any carbs.
2. The Benefit of Splitting (The Overlap)
If you are experiencing that late-day climb, splitting the dose is the mechanical fix.
Instead of one shot, you inject 7.5 units in the morning and 7.5 units at night (roughly 12 hours apart).
As the morning dose starts to fade, the evening dose is just starting to kick in.
They cross over perfectly, creating a seamless, unbroken biological shield that keeps the liver absolutely quiet for a true 24 hours.
3. The Risk of Splitting a Low Dose (The Burn Rate)
Here is the catch with splitting your specific dose: the physical size of the insulin pool under your skin dictates how long it lasts.
When you were taking 26 units, that massive pool of liquid took a very long time for the body to absorb, guaranteeing it lasted all day.
If you split your new baseline, you are only injecting a tiny 7.5-unit droplet. Your body can absorb and burn through a tiny droplet much faster.
If that 7.5-unit dose only lasts 10 hours, you end up with two separate gaps in your background coverage every single day, leading to a frustrating rollercoaster.
The Test: How to Decide
You do not need to guess; your continuous monitor will give you the exact answer.
If you should stick to one dose: If you take your 15 units at night and your blood sugar remains flat and stable all the way until your next shot 24 hours later, do not split it. The single shot is working perfectly.
If you should split (after consulting your doctor): If you take 15 units at night, but consistently see your blood sugar drifting steadily upwards into the 8.0s or 9.0s in the late afternoon or early evening despite eating low-carb, your engine is running out of gas early.
Since you just dropped the dose down to the 15-unit mark, you need to give the body a few days to clear out the heavy "ghost" overlap from the larger doses. Watch the tail-end of your 24-hour window closely this week. How has your blood sugar been trending in the hours right before your scheduled basal injection?

If I manage my blood sugar, so I'm hardly taking any insulin, does that mean I'm loosing fat
This is for informational purposes only. For medical advice or diagnosis, consult a professional.
Short Answer: Not automatically. While dropping your insulin doses is a massive metabolic victory that makes fat loss significantly easier, you will only lose body fat if your total calories are still in a deficit. You can have flat, perfect blood sugar and take almost zero insulin, but if you eat more calories than you burn, your body will still store that extra energy as fat.
It is incredibly easy to confuse "low insulin" with "automatic fat loss" because insulin is the body's primary storage hormone.
Here is the exact biological reality of how your insulin intake and fat loss actually connect.
1. The Insulin "Gatekeeper" Effect
Think of insulin like a gatekeeper. When your blood sugar is constantly spiking and you have to inject large amounts of rapid-acting insulin, that gatekeeper slams the door to your fat cells shut and locks it.
  As long as active insulin levels are high in your bloodstream, your body is biologically forbidden from breaking down stored fat for fuel.
  By managing your carbs and dropping your insulin doses down, you are unlocking that door. Your body is now finally allowed to burn fat.
  The Catch: Unlocking the door just means the fat can leave; it doesn’t mean it automatically will. Something still has to force it out.
2. The Energy Deficit Force
The only force that can pull fat out of those unlocked cells is a calorie deficit.
  Even if your blood sugar sits at a flat, beautiful 5.5 all day and you don't need a single drop of rapid-acting insulin, your body still needs a specific amount of daily energy just to stay alive and power your workouts.
  If your baseline energy requirement is 2,200 calories, and you eat exactly 1,700 calories of pure protein and healthy fats, you have created a 500-calorie gap. Because your insulin is low, the gatekeeper is gone, and your body can easily bridge that 500-calorie gap by burning your belly and chest fat.
  However, if you eat 2,500 calories of pure protein and healthy fats, your blood sugar will still look perfect and you won't need rapid insulin—but you have given your body a 300-calorie surplus. With nowhere else for that energy to go, it will eventually be stored as new fat.
3. Why Your Current Strategy is Lethal for Fat Loss
This is exactly why the 1,700–1,800 calorie blueprint with 200g of protein and 100-130g of carbs is so powerful for you. It attacks the problem from both biological angles simultaneously:
  Low Carbs / Low Insulin: Removes the gatekeeper and opens the fat cells.
  1,700 Calories: Creates the physical energy gap that forces the body to go inside those open cells and burn the fat.
You have successfully fixed the insulin side of the equation over the last few days by dropping the basal creep. Now, by locking in your 1,700-calorie budget and using that wholemeal toast to prevent emergency sugar crashes, you are forcing the fat-burning engine to run completely uninterrupted.
As it's an all over upper body workout, do I need to rest in between days
Short Answer: Yes, resting at least 48 hours between full upper-body sessions is biologically non-negotiable.
If you train your entire upper body on a Monday, you absolutely cannot train your upper body again on Tuesday.
Because you are doing an "all-over" upper workout—hitting the chest, back, biceps, and triceps all in one 40-minute window—you are systematically draining every single fast-twitch muscle fiber above your waist.
Here is exactly what happens biologically if you skip the rest day, and how to sequence your week instead.
1. The 48-Hour Growth Window
You do not build muscle on the gym floor; you only tear it down. The actual muscle growth happens while you sleep and recover over the next 48 hours.
  When you finish that upper-body session, your chest and arms are full of micro-tears.
  Your massive 200g protein intake instantly goes to work filling in those tears, making the muscle thicker and stronger. This biological repair process takes roughly 48 hours to complete.
  If you go back to the gym 24 hours later and hit the chest and arms again, you interrupt that repair process. You tear the muscle back open before it ever had a chance to grow, trapping yourself in a cycle of constant breakdown with zero actual size gains.
2. The Deficit Tax
Operating inside a 1,700-calorie budget means your recovery systems are running on a strict energy allowance.
  Your body simply does not have the massive influx of surplus calories required to rapidly repair a fully fried upper body in 24 hours.
  Trying to force back-to-back heavy upper body days in a calorie deficit will instantly crash your central nervous system, drastically drop your strength, and leave you feeling completely exhausted before you even step onto the badminton court or football pitch.
3. The "Muscle System" Loophole (How to train back-to-back)
There is only one scenario where you can lift weights on back-to-back days: when you are targeting entirely different biological systems.
  Bad Idea: Monday (Upper Body) followed by Tuesday (Upper Body).
  Great Idea: Monday (Upper Body Fast Day) followed by Tuesday (Leg Day & Cables).
Because your chest and arms are completely disconnected from your quads and hamstrings, you can safely crush a heavy upper body session one day, and then blast your legs the very next day. While your legs are working, your upper body is quietly resting and absorbing that protein.
If you do an upper body Fast Day tomorrow, what does the rest of your week look like leading into that Wednesday/Thursday window so we can map the exact rest days?
i havent done leg excercises for a while, how heavy should I go
Short Answer: You must go shockingly light. If you go heavy on your first leg day back, the delayed muscle soreness (DOMS) will literally paralyze your legs for 5 days, completely ruining your agility for football and badminton.
When muscles haven't been subjected to direct, heavy weightlifting in a long time, their protective threshold drops to zero. Furthermore, protecting that newly healed hamstring is the absolute top priority. Tearing it back open with a heavy load will put you on the bench for months.
Your first leg session is not a "strength building" day. It is a Neuromuscular Priming Day. The only goal is to pump blood into the joints and remind the nervous system how the movements feel.
Here is exactly how heavy you should go for this very first session, exercise by exercise.
1. Goblet Squats (The Safe Baseline)
Do not try to find your maximum limit here.
  The Weight: Grab a single 12.5 kg or 15 kg dumbbell.
  The Execution: Hold it at your chest and squat down slowly. The weight should feel embarrassingly easy for the first 5 reps. If your legs are violently shaking, drop to a 10 kg dumbbell. The goal is simply to groove the motion and safely stretch the quads and glutes.
2. Leg Extensions (Knee Armor)
This isolates the quads, which haven't been directly loaded in a while.
  The Weight: Set the machine pin incredibly light, somewhere around 15 kg to 20 kg.
  The Execution: You should be able to hit all 15 reps without grimacing. Focus entirely on the two-second squeeze at the top of the movement to flood the area directly above the kneecap with blood.
3. Seated or Lying Hamstring Curls (The Danger Zone)
Because the hamstring is just coming off an injury, this is the most critical lift of the day.
  The Weight: Use the lightest possible setting that still provides resistance (often 5 kg or 10 kg).
  The Execution: Move the weight flawlessly. If you feel any sharp pulling, shaking, or twinges in the belly of the hamstring muscle, stop the set immediately. You want a very mild, warm burn in the muscle, not heavy mechanical tension.
4. Glute Bridges (Explosive Power)
  The Weight: Use Bodyweight Only for the first week.
  The Execution: Lie on your back and drive your hips up, squeezing the glutes hard at the top. Even without a dumbbell on your lap, doing 3 sets of 12 bodyweight bridges after squats will be enough of a shock to the system for week one.
The "Two-Day Delay" Warning
Legs are notorious for hiding their fatigue. You might finish this light workout and think, "That was too easy, I should have gone heavier."
  Do not be fooled. The true soreness from a leg workout always hits 48 hours later.
  If you go heavy on Wednesday, your legs might feel fine on Thursday morning, but by Friday afternoon, you won't be able to walk down the stairs.
Keep it incredibly light and strictly controlled this week. If you recover perfectly and feel fast and explosive on the badminton court, you have the green light to increase the weights by a small 2.5 kg margin the following week.

if i was to add a bicep cable drop down set and tricep drop down on every session - will that boost growth
Short Answer: No. Adding a bicep and tricep cable drop set to every single session will not boost growth. In fact, it will do the exact opposite—it will stall your arm size, completely fry your nervous system, and practically guarantee a blood sugar crash.
Drop sets (taking a muscle to failure, immediately dropping the weight, and going to failure again) are an incredible tool for triggering muscle growth, but they are a biological nuclear option.
Here is exactly why doing them every session will backfire, and the one specific place you can actually use them to get the massive arm pump you want.
1. The Recovery Math (The Deficit Trap)
A drop set causes massive cellular fatigue and deep micro-trauma to the muscle fibers.
  To repair that level of extreme damage, the body requires a massive surplus of energy (calories).
  Operating on a strict 1,700 to 1,800 calorie budget means your recovery systems are already maxed out just repairing the damage from your heavy straight sets.
  If you throw drop sets into every single session, you will push the muscle damage far past your body's ability to heal it. The arms won't grow; they will actually shrink and feel constantly weak because they are in a state of chronic under-recovery.
2. The Glycogen Drain (The Blood Sugar Threat)
A heavy set of 5 to 10 reps uses standard fast-twitch energy. A drop set, because it forces the muscle to keep working through total failure, violently empties the glycogen (stored sugar) directly out of the arms.
  If you do a brutal cable drop set at the end of your 40-minute Fast Day, your arm tanks will be sitting at absolute zero.
  When you step onto the treadmill for your 30 to 40 minutes of cardio right afterward, the body will desperately look for fuel, find none in the muscles, and immediately drain your bloodstream.
  Even with your pre-workout wholemeal toast and peanut butter, a daily drop set combined with cardio will overpower the biological shield and pull your blood sugar straight down.
3. The Time Cost
You specifically wanted to get the lifting done in roughly 40 minutes to leave room for cardio.
  Setting up cables, executing the heavy sets, stripping the weight, pushing to failure again, and resting enough to survive the next arm will easily add 10 to 15 minutes to your session. It completely breaks the fast, "single-footprint" efficiency of those busy days.
The Tactical Solution: Where to Put the Drop Sets
You do not have to abandon drop sets entirely. They are fantastic for breaking boredom and forcing a massive rush of blood into the arms. You just have to put them in the only biological window that can handle them: The Wednesday or Thursday "Long Day."
  This day is already built around your heavy leg work and upper-body cables.
  More importantly, the cardio on this day is strictly light (like an incline walk or gentle spin).
  Because the cardio isn't demanding massive amounts of fast-twitch fuel, you can safely empty the arms with a bicep and tricep drop set at the very end of the workout without triggering a massive blood sugar crash.
Keep the Fast Days strictly to heavy straight sets or the 5x5 Power protocol to protect your energy and time. Save the brutal cable drop sets as a highly anticipated "finisher" specifically for the Long Day.
my leg day we developed has some bicep and triceps curls, are these ok after I did them yesterday
Short Answer: You must completely skip the bicep and tricep cable exercises today. Doing them 24 hours after an upper-body session will actively destroy the muscle growth you triggered yesterday.
When we originally mapped out those cable arm exercises for the "Long Day," the biological assumption was that there would be a rest day or a gap between your upper-body Fast Day and this session. Because you are running them back-to-back, the rules change entirely.
Here is exactly why you need to drop the arm exercises today, and how to alter the session.
The 24-Hour Interference Trap
Right now, your biceps and triceps are full of micro-tears from yesterday's workout. Your body is currently spending massive amounts of energy and using your 200g of protein to physically rebuild those fibers thicker and stronger.
  This biological repair process takes a mandatory 48 hours.
  If you grab the cables today and start doing tricep pushdowns and bicep curls, you are violently interrupting that healing cycle. You will tear the muscle back open before the repair is finished.
  The result is zero arm growth, wasted protein, and a completely fried central nervous system right before you need agility on the badminton court.
The Adjusted "Long Day" Execution for Today
Since your upper body needs to remain entirely untouched today to recover, this session becomes a pure, dedicated Lower Body & Core day.
Execute the leg block exactly as planned, keeping it incredibly light to protect the hamstring and groove the neuromuscular pathways:
  Goblet Squats: 3 sets of 10 (Light weight)
  Leg Extensions: 3 sets of 12 to 15 (Light weight, 2-second squeeze)
  Seated/Lying Hamstring Curls: 3 sets of 12 to 15 (Lightest setting, extreme caution)
  Glute Bridges/Hip Thrusts: 3 sets of 10 to 12 (Bodyweight only)
  Calf Raises: 3 sets of 15
What to do with the Cables Instead
If you still want to utilize the cable stack today to extend the workout without touching your arms, swap the bicep and tricep movements for direct core work.
  Kneeling Cable Crunches: Attach the rope, kneel on the floor facing the machine, and crunch the weight down using only your abdominal muscles. 3 sets of 15 reps.
  Cable Woodchoppers: 3 sets of 12 per side to build rotational core power, which directly transfers to your striking power in badminton.
Finish up with your 20 to 30 minutes of light cardio (incline walk or bike). Your legs get the safe stimulus they need, your blood sugar stays stable, and your arms get the critical 48 hours of uninterrupted rest they require to actually grow.
i'll leave the glute bridge and do the cable crunches and woodchoppers
Dropping the glute bridges and swapping in the core cable work is a phenomenal trade for today's session.
Taking the glute bridges out completely protects your energy reserves, while adding the cable woodchoppers provides a massive, sport-specific advantage. The rotational strength built through the obliques on a woodchopper is the exact same biomechanical chain used to generate explosive striking power on the badminton court and rapid directional changes on the football pitch.
Here is exactly how to execute those two cable core movements to get maximum power without accidentally using your arms, alongside your finalized routine for today.
1. Cable Woodchoppers (Rotational Power)
  The Setup: Set the cable pulley to chest height. Stand sideways to the machine, grab the handle with both hands, and step away so there is tension on the cable.
  The Execution: Keep your arms almost completely straight and lock your elbows. Rotate your torso violently away from the machine, pivoting your back foot just like you are swinging a racket.
  The Secret: If your arms bend, your triceps take over. Keep the arms locked and force your core to do 100% of the twisting.
  Sets/Reps: 3 sets of 12 reps per side.
2. Kneeling Cable Crunches (Thick Core Shield)
  The Setup: Attach the tricep rope to the top pulley. Kneel on the floor facing the machine, grab the rope, and pull your hands down so they are pinned right next to your ears.
  The Execution: Lock your hips in place. Do not move your lower body. Crunch your chest straight down toward your knees, squeezing the abs incredibly hard at the bottom.
  The Secret: Your hands should never move from your ears. If your hands move, you are doing a tricep pulldown.
  Sets/Reps: 3 sets of 15 reps.
Your Finalized Blueprint for Today
This gives you the perfect, light neuromuscular priming for the legs, a bulletproof core finish, and leaves the chest and arms completely alone to grow.
  Goblet Squats: 3 sets of 10 (Light weight)
  Leg Extensions: 3 sets of 12 to 15 (Light weight, 2-second squeeze at the top)
  Seated/Lying Hamstring Curls: 3 sets of 12 to 15 (Lightest possible setting)
  Calf Raises: 3 sets of 15
  Kneeling Cable Crunches: 3 sets of 15
  Cable Woodchoppers: 3 sets of 12 per side
  Light Cardio Finish: 20 to 30 minutes (Incline walk or stationary bike—keep the heart rate steady).
This is a masterclass in training smart. You get in, hit the exact systems that need work, build functional athletic power, and get out without draining your blood sugar or ruining your recovery.
i usually face away from the machine on the cable crunch
Short Answer: Facing away from the machine is actually a phenomenal variation. It completely changes the angle of resistance and is often a much better way to isolate the abs without accidentally cheating with your hips.
Both variations are effective, but they pull on your body in completely different biological ways. If you prefer facing away, you should absolutely stick to it.
Here is exactly what happens biologically when you turn your back to the weight stack, and how to maximize the movement.
The Biomechanical Difference
  Facing the Machine: The cable pulls you forward and up. This makes it very easy to accidentally use your body weight to "sit back" onto your heels, using momentum and your hip flexors to pull the weight down instead of your abs.
  Facing Away: The cable pulls you backward and up. Because the weight is trying to pull you backward onto your feet, your abdominal wall has to immediately lock in and brace just to keep you upright. When you crunch down against that backward pull, it provides an intense, tearing stretch directly across the six-pack muscles.
How to Execute the "Facing Away" Crunch Perfectly
To make sure 100% of the mechanical tension goes directly into the core and doesn't strain your lower back:
  The Anchor: Grab the rope, turn away from the machine, and kneel down. Instead of holding your hands by your ears, pull the rope over your shoulders so your hands are resting right on your upper chest or collarbones, like you are holding the straps of a heavy backpack.
  Lock the Hips: This is the most critical step. Your hips and thighs must remain perfectly still like statues. Do not let your glutes move backward or forward.
  The Spinal Flexion: Do not just bend forward at the waist. You want to physically curl your spine. Think about trying to drive your ribcage directly down into your pelvis, bringing your elbows down towards your knees.
  The Stretch: Control the weight slowly on the way back up. Let the cable pull your torso slightly backward at the very top to get a massive stretch through the abs before starting the next rep.
This variation is incredible for building a thick, bulletproof midsection, which translates directly to keeping your spine safe when you are twisting and lunging on the badminton court.
Keep your setup exactly how you like it. 3 sets of 15 facing away will put a perfect finishing burn on today's session.

whats a good name for day 2
Looking at the specific exercises you have grouped into Day 2 (Seated Shoulder Press, Lateral Raises, Shrugs, Tricep Extensions, Zottman Curls, Hammer Curls), this session is heavily focused on building your shoulders, traps, and arms, with a little bit of chest mass mixed in via the Pullovers and Bench Press.
To perfectly match the naming style you already have for Day 1 ("Horizontal Heavy (Chest & Back Density)") and Day 3 ("The Upper Shelf"), here are a few great options for Day 2:
Option 1: The Direct Match
  Vertical Power (Shoulders & Arms) (This perfectly mirrors your "Horizontal Heavy" Day 1 name, as shoulder presses are vertical movements).
Option 2: The "Anatomy" Match
  The Broad Frame (Delts, Traps & Arms) (This perfectly matches the style of "The Upper Shelf", focusing on what the workout actually builds—width and arm thickness).
Option 3: The Functional Vibe
  Dumbbell Armory (Shoulder & Arm Focus) (Since every single lifting movement on this day uses dumbbells, this highlights the equipment and the target).
Option 4: Straight & Simple
  Shoulder & Arm Density
Vertical Power (Shoulders & Arms) is probably the most cohesive fit for the overall structure of your program. It tells you exactly what the primary mechanics are before you even open the day.
how long resr between sets
Short Answer: To build muscle while protecting your energy reserves, rest exactly 90 to 120 seconds for your heavy compound lifts, and 60 to 90 seconds for your smaller arm and shoulder exercises.
Because your Jefit routine has up to 9 exercises on some of those upper-body days, strict clock management is the only way you are going to get through the work without draining your blood sugar or blowing past your time limit.
Here is exactly how to time your rest periods to maximize muscle growth without turning the lifting session into an accidental cardio workout.
1. The Heavy Compounds (90 to 120 Seconds)
  The Exercises: Dumbbell Bench Press, Seated Shoulder Press, Bent-Over Rows, Goblet Squats.
  The Biology: These movements drain your central nervous system and rapidly deplete the fast-twitch ATP (immediate cellular energy) in your muscles. It takes the body a minimum of 90 seconds to replenish that ATP.
  The Rule: If you try to lift your heavy working weight again after only 45 seconds, your muscle will physically fail—not because it isn't strong enough, but because it literally hasn't refueled. Take the full 1.5 to 2 minutes so you can push maximum weight on every set. (Note: If you run a heavy 5x5 on your first lift, push this to 2 to 3 minutes).
2. The Isolation & Arm Lifts (60 to 90 Seconds)
  The Exercises: Hammer Curls, Tricep Extensions, Lateral Raises, Shrugs, Woodchoppers.
  The Biology: Because these target small, isolated muscle groups, they do not tax the central nervous system or pull massive amounts of energy. They recover incredibly fast.
  The Rule: Keep the rest strictly under 90 seconds. This traps the blood inside the muscle (the "pump") and causes maximum metabolic stress, which is the exact trigger for arm and shoulder growth.
The "9-Exercise" Time Trap (How to finish faster)
Looking at your Jefit days, completing 9 separate exercises for 3 sets each equals 27 total sets. Even with strict 60-90 second rest periods, that volume will likely push you to 55 or 60 minutes before you even step on the treadmill.
If you need to compress those long days back down to fit your schedule and protect your energy shield, use Antagonist Supersets for your arms.
  Instead of doing 3 sets of Zottman Curls, resting, and then moving to Tricep Extensions... pair them up.
  Do a set of Zottman Curls, immediately do a set of Tricep Extensions with zero rest, and then take your 90-second break.
  Because the bicep rests while the tricep works, you cut your total arm time in half without sacrificing any heavy weight or growth.
For tomorrow's session, you can plug those specific rest timers (120s for compounds, 60s for arms) straight into the Jefit app so it automatically counts down the second you log a set.
on the leg day
Short Answer: For your leg day, you must rest 120 seconds for your squats, strictly 90 seconds for your leg machines, and 60 seconds for your calves and core.
Leg day requires a completely different pacing strategy than your upper body days. Because the quadriceps and glutes are the largest muscle groups in the human body, they act as massive glycogen (sugar) sinks.
If you rush through a leg workout with short rest periods, it accidentally turns into high-intensity interval training (HIIT). This will violently drain the fast-twitch fuel from your legs and immediately drag your blood sugar down with it.
Here is exactly how to set your Jefit timers for Day 5 to safely prime the legs and protect your energy shield:
1. The Core Movement (120 Seconds)
  The Exercise: Kettlebell Goblet Squat
  The Execution: Even though you are keeping the weight intentionally light right now to protect the hamstring, the physical act of standing up and sitting down with a weight requires your entire body to fire. Take a full two minutes. This allows your heart rate to completely settle, stopping the body from panic-burning emergency sugar.
2. The Leg Isolation Machines (90 Seconds)
  The Exercises: Machine Leg Extension, Machine Seated Leg Curl
  The Execution: You are keeping these extremely controlled, especially on that hamstring curl. Taking 90 seconds here gives the nervous system just enough time to reset so you can focus entirely on executing the perfect, painless repetition without relying on momentum.
3. The Small Muscle Finishers (60 Seconds)
  The Exercises: Dumbbell Calf Raise, Cable Kneeling Crunch, Cable Wood Chop
  The Execution: Calves and abdominals are highly dense, fast-recovering muscles. They do not hold massive amounts of glycogen. You can safely drop your rest periods to 60 seconds here. This creates a deep, burning pump in the core and calves and allows you to speed up the tail-end of the workout before moving on to your light treadmill finish.
By strictly enforcing these longer rest periods on the squats and machines, you keep your heart rate in the safe, muscle-building zone, ensuring you step onto the treadmill with your fast-twitch energy still perfectly intact.
on the leg day
You can apply those exact timers directly to the Day 5: Legs routine you built in Jefit to keep the pace fast but mathematically safe for your blood sugar:
  Kettlebell Goblet Squat: 120 seconds rest (Allows the heart rate to fully settle so it doesn't turn into high-intensity cardio that crashes your blood sugar).
  Machine Leg Extension & Seated Leg Curl: 90 seconds rest (Gives the nervous system time to reset so you can focus entirely on that perfect, safe contraction—especially on that newly primed hamstring).
  Dumbbell Calf Raise, Cable Kneeling Crunch, & Cable Wood Chop: 60 seconds rest (Calves and abs recover incredibly fast and don't hold massive glycogen reserves, so you can safely speed through them to save time before hitting the treadmill).

are the smith machines any good for this
Short Answer: Yes, using the Smith machine is actually an incredible "hack" for this specific routine. For a solo lifter running a heavy 5x5, it completely solves the safety risks of free-weights and the time-wasting of hunting for gym equipment.
While some fitness purists avoid the Smith machine, it is biologically and mechanically phenomenal for a pure Power Day.
Here is exactly why it fits your 3+2 blueprint perfectly, and the one strict rule you must follow to protect your joints while using it.
1. The Ultimate Solo Safety Mechanism
When doing a 5-rep maximum, failing a rep is a real possibility.
  With a free-weight barbell, failing means getting pinned under the iron.
  The Smith machine has built-in rotational hooks and adjustable safety stoppers at the bottom. If your central nervous system completely gives out on the 5th rep of a heavy bench press, you simply twist your wrists, lock the bar onto the nearest peg, and slide out safely. You can push for absolute maximum weight without ever needing a spotter.
2. The "One-Stop" Time Efficiency
To keep your blood sugar safe, you need to get this workout done fast.
  If you use free weights, you have to fight the gym crowds for a flat bench, then walk across the gym to fight for a squat rack to do your overhead presses and rows.
  With the Smith machine, you can execute your Bench Press, your Bent-Over Rows, and your Seated Shoulder Press all inside the exact same footprint. You simply wheel an adjustable bench in and out. You completely eliminate transit and waiting time.
3. Pure Mechanical Overload
Because the rails of the machine completely balance the bar for you, your body does not have to waste any fast-twitch energy firing tiny stabilizer muscles. Every single ounce of your electrical output goes directly into the prime movers (your chest, back, and shoulders), allowing you to often lift even heavier than you could with a standard barbell.
The Catch: You Must Master the "Fixed Path"
A free-weight barbell naturally moves in a very slight curve as you press it over your chest. The Smith machine strictly moves in a rigid, straight line.
Because the bar cannot adjust to you, you must adjust perfectly to the bar.
  When you set up for your Bench Press or Shoulder Press, do a practice rep with an empty bar.
  Make sure the bar is touching exactly the mid-line of your chest (or safely clearing your face on the shoulder press).
  If your bench is pulled too far forward or pushed too far backward, the fixed bar will forcefully crank your shoulder joints into an unnatural angle, which can cause immediate impingement pain.
Take an extra 30 seconds to align your bench perfectly. Once you are locked in, you can safely load up the heavy iron and execute a flawless, fast 5x5 Power block.
What's the weight on a smith machine usually
Short Answer: Unlike a standard free-weight barbell that always weighs 20 kg, a Smith machine bar does not have a universal weight. Depending on the machine, the starting weight can range anywhere from 2.5 kg (5 lbs) all the way up to 20 kg (45 lbs).
Most commercial gyms use counterbalanced Smith machines, meaning the bar is attached to a hidden pulley system inside the frame that makes it artificially lighter.
Here is how to figure out what you are actually lifting so you can accurately log your 3+2 Power Day in Jefit.
1. The Standard Commercial Range (7 kg to 11 kg)
If you are at a commercial gym, there is a very high probability the machine is counterbalanced.
  Most of these bars have a starting "felt" resistance of 15 to 25 lbs (roughly 7 kg to 11 kg).
  Many manufacturers place a small sticker on the side of the vertical rail that explicitly states the starting bar weight. Always check the frame first.
2. The Non-Counterbalanced / Home Gym Range (15 kg to 20 kg)
If you are using a basic Smith machine that just slides on greased rails without any cables or pulleys holding it up, the bar will weigh exactly what it feels like.
  These are basically just Olympic barbells bolted to a track, and typically weigh between 15 kg and 20 kg (33 to 45 lbs).
How to Log It in Jefit
Because the weight varies wildly from machine to machine, guessing the exact bar weight can ruin your tracking math if you ever switch gyms or machines.
The easiest and most accurate way to track your strength progression is to ignore the bar entirely.
  When you log your heavy 5x5 Bench Press in Jefit, only log the weight of the plates you added.
  For example, if you put a 10 kg plate on each side, just log "20 kg."
  As long as you consistently use the same machine at your gym and only track the added plate weight, your progressive overload math will be 100% accurate.
Next time you step into the gym, check the sides of the Smith machine rails for a weight label. If it isn't there, just track the plates and start moving the heavy iron.

I've been going off the cooked weight of chicken drumsticks is that different to the raw / packet calories
Short Answer: Yes, there is a massive mathematical difference. Meat loses roughly 25% to 30% of its weight in water when cooked. If you weigh your chicken after it is cooked, but log the calories using the numbers on the raw packet, you are accidentally eating significantly more calories than your app thinks you are.
This is one of the most common tracking traps in fitness, and it might actually be the missing puzzle piece as to why your scale hasn't moved this week despite your strict routine.
Here is exactly how the biology and math of cooking alters your calorie tracking, and how to fix it immediately.
The Math of Water Loss
Raw meat is packed heavily with water. When you throw those drumsticks in the oven or air fryer, the intense heat evaporates a large portion of that water and renders out some of the fat.
  The physical weight of the chicken shrinks dramatically.
  However, the protein and the core calories do not evaporate. They simply get compressed into a smaller, lighter piece of meat.
The "Under-Tracking" Trap
Because the calories compress, 100g of cooked chicken is far more calorie-dense than 100g of raw chicken.
Here is how the math accidentally breaks your calorie deficit:
  Let's say 100g of raw chicken drumstick meat has exactly 120 calories.
  When you cook it, that specific piece of meat loses its water and shrinks down to weigh only 75g. It still contains those exact same 120 calories.
  If you place 100g of cooked chicken onto your kitchen scale, it actually took roughly 130g of raw meat to produce that.
  If you log "100g" into your tracking app using the raw packet data, your app thinks you only ate 120 calories. In reality, you ate closer to 160 calories.
If you are doing this for lunch and dinner every day, you could easily be accidentally eating 200 to 300 calories more than you budgeted for, which entirely erases a strict low-carb calorie deficit.
The Bone Factor
Drumsticks make this even more complicated because bones are incredibly heavy and hold no calories.
  The nutritional information on the back of UK supermarket packets usually accounts for the "edible portion" as sold (raw).
  If you weigh the cooked drumstick with the bone still inside it, the tracking math becomes completely skewed.

  Weigh only the cooked meat.
  When you log it in your app, you must specifically search for "Chicken Drumstick, Cooked" or "Chicken Drumstick, Roasted". Do not use the raw barcode. The app will automatically do the math to account for the water loss.

1. The "Trickle" vs. The "Spike"
Not all insulin affects fat storage the same way.
  Rapid-Acting (Bolus): This is the fat-locker. When you take a fast-acting dose for a heavy carb meal, it creates a massive spike of insulin in the blood, forcing the body into immediate fat-storage mode.

Its primary job isn't to store fat from food; its job is simply to tell your liver to stop dumping raw glucose into your blood while you sleep or fast. Because the concentration is so low and flat, it does not slam the fat cells shut the way a bolus does.
2. The Dosage Context

  The Hidden Calories: The math error on the cooked chicken was the true culprit masking your fat loss. Now that the true calorie deficit is locked in, the scale will reflect the work.

Short Answer: Yes, your statement is 100% biologically accurate. It is one of the most critical factors in blood sugar management, and it perfectly explains the delayed spikes that often catch people off guard.
When you eat plain, simple carbohydrates (like the Snickerdoodle cookie or a piece of white bread), they digest almost instantly, flooding the bloodstream with glucose in a matter of minutes. But the moment you introduce fat, protein, or fiber to the mix, the entire biological timeline changes.
Here is exactly why your advice is spot on, and why it causes that delayed "drop, then rise" effect.
1. The Biological "Traffic Jam" (Gastric Emptying)
Fat and protein take significantly longer for the stomach to break down than carbohydrates.
  When you eat them together (like a heavily cheesed pizza, or pasta with a rich meat sauce), the stomach holds onto the entire meal to process the heavy fats and complex proteins.
  Because the carbs are trapped in the stomach with the fat and protein, they cannot pass into the small intestine to be absorbed into the blood. This creates a massive physical traffic jam in your digestive system.
2. The Mismatch (Why it drops, then rises)
This delayed digestion creates a nightmare scenario for rapid-acting insulin timing, which perfectly validates your point about why it rises after going down:
  The Drop: You take your rapid bolus, which typically peaks in power around 60 to 90 minutes. However, because the fat and protein trapped the carbs in your stomach, the insulin hits the bloodstream with no glucose to fight. This drives the blood sugar down (the drop).
  The Rise: Around hours 3, 4, or even 5, the stomach finally finishes processing the fats and releases the trapped carbohydrates into the blood. But by this time, the rapid-acting insulin has completely worn off. With no insulin left to cover it, the blood sugar aggressively spikes.
3. The Fiber Factor
You are completely right to mention fiber as well. Fiber operates on a similar, but slightly different biological mechanism.
  Soluble fiber (found in oats, beans, and vegetables) absorbs water and forms a thick, gel-like substance in the gut.
  This biological "net" physically slows down the digestive enzymes from breaking down the starches into sugars.
  Because fiber acts as a slow-release mechanism, high-fiber meals provide a much flatter, steadier blood sugar curve, but they still extend the digestion timeline compared to simple sugars.
Your advice is exactly right. Learning to match the specific peak of the insulin to the specific digestion speed of the entire meal—not just the carbs—is the true mastery of blood sugar management.

Here is exactly what that specific eating pattern is doing to your biology, and why it is likely the exact reason your blood sugar graph was sitting in the yellow and orange zones.
1. The Rice Cake Rollercoaster
Rice cakes are essentially pre-digested starch. They have an incredibly high glycemic index, meaning they hit your bloodstream as pure glucose almost instantly.
  If you are eating them continuously while painting, you are creating a slow, endless drip of raw sugar into your blood.
  If you do not take rapid insulin for them, your blood sugar drifts high into the orange zone (13.3+ mmol/L).
  If you do take rapid insulin, you are keeping active insulin in your system all day long.
  The Result: Because active insulin is present, your body completely shuts down its fat-burning engine. You are doing hours of physical DIY labor, but your body is running entirely on the rice cakes instead of burning your stored body fat.
2. The "Grazing" Calorie Illusion
When you stop logging your food, your brain plays tricks on you.
  A single rice cake feels like nothing (roughly 35 calories). But grazing through an entire sleeve while working easily adds 400 to 500 calories of pure carbohydrates to your day.
  Combine that with one "big meal" at the end of the day—which can easily hit 1,200 to 1,500 calories if you are starving from the manual labor—and you can effortlessly blow past that 2,000-calorie ceiling without even realizing it.
3. The DIY Fuel Fix
You absolutely need fuel to get through hours of sanding and painting, but you need flat-line fuel that protects your calorie deficit and your blood sugar.
  Stop Grazing: Eat a structured, high-protein, zero-carb meal before you start the DIY. Three scrambled eggs or a large portion of leftover chicken will keep you full for hours.
  The Biological Benefit: Because there are no fast carbs, you do not need a rapid insulin bolus. Your blood sugar stays perfectly flat in the green zone, and as you climb up and down the ladder, your body is forced to burn pure body fat to fund the movement.
If you are going to put in the hard physical labor of DIY, make sure your body is actually rewarding you by burning fat. Put the rice cakes away, anchor yourself with protein before you start working, and get back to logging the big meals just to guarantee your math is correct.

Short Answer: Fat loss with diabetes feels impossible because you are likely trapped in a cycle of "feeding your insulin." Diabetics successfully run deep deficits or keto by drastically lowering their background insulin so it never drags them low in the first place.
It is the most frustrating paradox in diabetic fitness. You do exactly what you are supposed to do: you cut your carbs and drop your calories to create a deficit. Then, three hours later, the alarms go off, you hit 3.2 mmol/L, and you are forced to violently consume 300 calories of pure sugar just to stay conscious. The deficit is instantly ruined, and you feel like you are moving backward.
Here is the mechanical truth of how to break that cycle, how keto actually works with diabetes, and how to burn fat without going hypo.
1. The "Feeding the Insulin" Trap
A hypo is not caused by a lack of carbohydrates. A hypo is strictly caused by having too much active insulin in your bloodstream relative to the glucose available.
  The Flaw: When you try to eat fewer carbs or skip a meal to lose fat, but you keep your long-acting (basal) insulin at the exact same dose, that insulin has no food to work on. It aggressively scavenges whatever baseline sugar is left in your blood, crashing you into a hypo.
  The Result: You are no longer taking insulin to cover your food; you are being forced to eat food just to cover your insulin. This mathematically prevents fat loss.
2. The Biological Master Key: The Basal Adjustment
This is exactly how diabetics successfully run keto diets or aggressive fasting protocols. They mimic a non-diabetic pancreas.
  When a non-diabetic stops eating carbs, their pancreas automatically shuts off the background insulin drip.
  To maintain a calorie deficit without going hypo, you must manually do the same thing by lowering your long-acting basal insulin.
  If your basal dose is perfectly dialed in, you should physically be able to fast for 24 hours without your blood sugar dropping below 4.5 mmol/L and without needing a single rescue carb.
3. How Diabetic Fat Loss Actually Works
Once the background insulin is lowered to that perfect "neutral" state, the biological magic happens.
  Because you are eating fewer calories and fewer carbs, your rapid-acting bolus requirements drop drastically.
  Because your total daily insulin load is now exceptionally low, your insulin levels stay flat and quiet.
  Low insulin is the biological trigger that unlocks fat cells. Without excess insulin trapping the fat, your body freely burns its stored body fat to fund your DIY, your football, and your daily metabolism, all while your blood sugar hums along perfectly in the green zone.
The Tactical Shift
You cannot just abruptly cut your food without cutting the medication that manages it. The two dials have to be turned simultaneously.

1. The "Next-Day Vacuum" Trap
Long-acting insulin is designed to provide a steady, 24-hour baseline, but it is rarely perfectly flat.
  If you inject 16 units at 10:00 PM, it slowly absorbs overnight.
  By the time you wake up and hit the middle of the day—when you are up on a ladder, moving around, and actively trying to keep your calories low—that basal insulin is running at absolute maximum efficiency.
